In [[mathematics]], the '''Segre class''' is a [[characteristic class]] used in the study of [[cone (algebraic geometry)|cone]]s, a generalization of [[vector bundle]]s. For vector bundles the total Segre class is inverse to the total [[Chern class]], and thus provides equivalent information; the advantage of the Segre class is that it generalizes to more general cones, while the Chern class does not.
The Segre class was introduced in the non-singular case by [[Beniamino Segre]] (1953).<ref>{{harvnb|Segre|1953}}</ref>
In the modern treatment of [[intersection theory]] in [[algebraic geometry]], as developed e.g. in the definitive book of Fulton (1998), Segre classes play a fundamental role.<ref name="Fulton 1998">{{harvnb|Fulton|1998}}</ref>

== Definition ==

Suppose that <math>C</math> is a [[cone (algebraic geometry)|cone]] over <math>X
</math>, that <math>q</math> is the projection from the [[projective completion of a cone|projective completion]] <math>\mathbb{P}(C \oplus 1)</math> of <math>C</math> to <math>X</math>, and that <math>\mathcal{O}(1)</math> is the [[anti-tautological line bundle]] on <math>\mathbb{P}(C \oplus 1)</math>. Viewing the [[Chern class]] <math>c_1(\mathcal{O}(1))</math> as a group endomorphism of the [[Chow group]] of <math>\mathbb{P}(C \oplus 1)</math>, the total Segre class of <math>C</math> is given by:
:<math>s(C) = q_* \left( \sum_{i \geq 0} c_1(\mathcal{O}(1))^{i} [\mathbb{P}(C \oplus 1)] \right).</math>
The <math>i</math>th Segre class <math>s_i(C)</math> is simply the <math>i</math>th graded piece of <math>s(C)</math>. If <math>C</math> is of pure dimension <math>r</math> over <math>X</math> then this is given by:
:<math>s_i(C) = q_* \left( c_1(\mathcal{O}(1))^{r+i} [\mathbb{P}(C \oplus 1)] \right).</math>

The reason for using <math>\mathbb{P}(C \oplus 1)</math> rather than <math>\mathbb{P}(C)</math> is that this makes the total Segre class stable under addition of the trivial bundle <math>\mathcal{O}</math>.

If ''Z'' is a closed subscheme of an algebraic scheme ''X'', then <math>s(Z, X)</math> denotes the Segre class of the [[normal cone (algebraic geometry)|normal cone]] to <math>Z \hookrightarrow X</math>.

===Relation to Chern classes for vector bundles===

For a [[holomorphic vector bundle]] <math>E</math> over a [[complex manifold]] <math>M</math> a total Segre class <math>s(E)</math> is the inverse to the total [[Chern class]] <math>c(E)</math>, see e.g. Fulton (1998).<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=p.50.}}</ref>

Explicitly, for a total Chern class

: <math> 
c(E) = 1+c_1(E) + c_2(E) + \cdots \,
</math>

one gets the total Segre class

: <math>
s(E) = 1 + s_1 (E) + s_2 (E) + \cdots \,
</math>

where

: <math>
c_1(E) = -s_1(E), \quad c_2(E) = s_1(E)^2 - s_2(E), \quad \dots, \quad c_n(E) = -s_1(E)c_{n-1}(E) - s_2(E) c_{n-2}(E) - \cdots - s_n(E) 
</math>

Let <math> x_1, \dots, x_k </math> be Chern roots, i.e. formal eigenvalues of <math> \frac{ i \Omega }{ 2\pi} </math> where <math> \Omega </math> is a curvature of a [[connection (mathematics)|connection]] on <math> E </math>.

While the Chern class c(E) is written as

:<math> c(E)  = \prod_{i=1}^{k} (1+x_i) = c_0 + c_1 + \cdots + c_k \, </math>

where <math> c_i </math> is an [[elementary symmetric polynomial]] of degree <math> i </math> in variables <math> x_1, \dots, x_k  </math>,

the Segre for the [[dual bundle]] <math> E^\vee </math> which has Chern roots <math> -x_1, \dots, -x_k </math> is written as

:<math> s(E^\vee) = \prod_{i=1}^{k} \frac {1} { 1 -  x_i } = s_0 + s_1 + \cdots </math>

Expanding the above expression in powers of <math> x_1, \dots x_k </math> one can see that <math>s_i (E^\vee) </math> is represented by
a [[complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial]] of <math> x_1, \dots x_k </math>.

== Properties ==
Here are some basic properties.
*For any cone ''C'' (e.g., a vector bundle), <math>s(C \oplus 1) = s(C)</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Example 4.1.1.}}</ref>
*For a cone ''C'' and a vector bundle ''E'',
*:<math>c(E)s(C \oplus E) = s(C).</math><ref>
{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Example 4.1.5.}}</ref>
*If ''E'' is a vector bundle, then<ref name=Fulton>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Proposition 3.1.}}</ref>
*:<math>s_i(E) = 0</math> for <math>i < 0</math>.
*:<math>s_0(E)</math> is the identity operator.
*:<math>s_i(E) \circ s_j(F) = s_j(F) \circ s_i(E)</math> for another vector bundle ''F''.
*If ''L'' is a line bundle, then <math>s_1(L) = -c_1(L)</math>, minus the first Chern class of ''L''.<ref name=Fulton />
*If ''E'' is a vector bundle of rank <math>e + 1</math>, then, for a line bundle ''L'',
*:<math>s_p(E \otimes L) = \sum_{i=0}^p (-1)^{p-i} \binom{e+p}{e+i} s_i(E) c_1(L)^{p-i}.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Example 3.1.1.}}</ref>

A key property of a Segre class is birational invariance: this is contained in the following. Let <math>p: X \to Y</math> be a [[proper morphism]] between [[algebraic scheme]]s such that <math>Y</math> is irreducible and each [[irreducible component]] of <math>X</math> maps onto <math>Y</math>. Then, for each closed subscheme <math>W \subset Y</math>, <math>V = p^{-1}(W)</math> and <math>p_V: V \to W</math> the restriction of <math>p</math>,
:<math>{p_V}_*(s(V, X)) = \operatorname{deg}(p) \, s(W, Y).</math><ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Proposition 4.2. (a)}}</ref>
Similarly, if <math>f: X \to Y</math> is a [[flat morphism]] of constant relative dimension between pure-dimensional algebraic schemes, then, for each closed subscheme <math>W \subset Y</math>, <math>V = f^{-1}(W)</math> and <math>f_V: V \to W</math> the restriction of <math>f</math>,
:<math>{f_V}^*(s(W, Y)) = s(V, X).</math><ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Proposition 4.2. (b)}}</ref>

A basic example of birational invariance is provided by a blow-up. Let <math>\pi: \widetilde{X} \to X</math> be a blow-up along some closed subscheme ''Z''. Since the [[exceptional divisor]] <math>E := \pi^{-1}(Z) \hookrightarrow \widetilde{X}</math> is an effective Cartier divisor and the normal cone (or normal bundle) to it is <math>\mathcal{O}_E(E) := \mathcal{O}_X(E)|_E</math>,
:<math>\begin{align}
s(E, \widetilde{X}) &= c(\mathcal{O}_E(E))^{-1} [E] \\
&= [E] - E \cdot [E] + E \cdot (E \cdot [E]) + \cdots,
\end{align}</math>
where we used the notation <math>D \cdot \alpha = c_1(\mathcal{O}(D))\alpha</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=§ 2.5.}}</ref> Thus,
:<math>s(Z, X) = g_* \left( \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{k-1} E^k \right)</math>
where <math>g: E = \pi^{-1}(Z) \to Z</math> is given by <math>\pi</math>.

== Examples ==

=== Example 1 ===
Let ''Z'' be a smooth curve that is a complete intersection of effective Cartier divisors <math>D_1, \dots, D_n</math> on a variety ''X''. Assume the dimension of ''X'' is ''n'' + 1. Then the Segre class of the [[normal cone]] <math>C_{Z/X}</math> to <math>Z \hookrightarrow X</math> is:<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Example 9.1.1.}}</ref>
:<math>s(C_{Z/X}) = [Z] - \sum_{i=1}^n D_i \cdot [Z].</math>
Indeed, for example, if ''Z'' is regularly embedded into ''X'', then, since <math>C_{Z/X} = N_{Z/X}</math> is the normal bundle and <math>N_{Z/X} = \bigoplus_{i=1}^n N_{D_i/X}|_Z</math> (see [[Normal cone#Properties]]), we have:
:<math>s(C_{Z/X}) = c(N_{Z/X})^{-1}[Z] = \prod_{i=1}^d (1-c_1(\mathcal{O}_X(D_i))) [Z] = [Z] - \sum_{i=1}^n D_i \cdot [Z].</math>

=== Example 2 ===
The following is Example 3.2.22. of Fulton (1998).<ref name="Fulton 1998"/> It recovers some classical results from Schubert's book on [[enumerative geometry]].

Viewing the dual [[projective space]] <math>\breve{\mathbb{P}^3}</math> as the [[Grassmann bundle]] <math>p: \breve{\mathbb{P}^3} \to *</math> parametrizing the 2-planes in <math>\mathbb{P}^3</math>, consider the tautological [[exact sequence]]
:<math>0 \to S \to p^* \mathbb{C}^3 \to Q \to 0</math>
where <math>S, Q</math> are the tautological sub and quotient bundles. With <math>E = \operatorname{Sym}^2(S^* \otimes Q^*)</math>, the [[projective bundle]] <math>q: X = \mathbb{P}(E) \to \breve{\mathbb{P}^3}</math> is the variety of conics in <math>\mathbb{P}^3</math>. With <math>\beta = c_1(Q^*)</math>, we have <math>c(S^* \otimes Q^*) = 2 \beta + 2\beta^2</math> and so, using [[Chern class#Computation formulae]],
:<math>c(E) = 1 + 8 \beta + 30 \beta^2 + 60 \beta^3</math>
and thus
:<math>s(E) = 1 + 8 h + 34 h^2 + 92 h^3</math>
where <math>h = -\beta = c_1(Q).</math> The coefficients in <math>s(E)</math> have the enumerative geometric meanings; for example, 92 is the number of conics meeting 8 general lines.

{{See also|Residual intersection#Example: conics tangent to given five conics}}

=== Example 3 ===
Let ''X'' be a surface and <math>A, B, D</math> effective Cartier divisors on it. Let <math>Z \subset X</math> be the [[scheme-theoretic intersection]] of <math>A + D</math> and <math>B + D</math> (viewing those divisors as closed subschemes). For simplicity, suppose <math>A, B</math> meet only at a single point ''P'' with the same multiplicity ''m'' and that ''P'' is a smooth point of ''X''. Then<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Example 4.2.2.}}</ref>
:<math>s(Z, X) = [D] + (m^2[P] - D \cdot [D]).</math>
To see this, consider the blow-up <math>\pi: \widetilde{X} \to X</math> of ''X'' along ''P'' and let <math>g: \widetilde{Z} = \pi^{-1}Z \to Z</math>, the strict transform of ''Z''. By the formula at [[#Properties]],
:<math>s(Z, X) = g_* ([\widetilde{Z}]) - g_*(\widetilde{Z} \cdot [\widetilde{Z}]).</math>
Since <math>\widetilde{Z} = \pi^* D + mE</math> where <math>E = \pi^{-1} P</math>, the formula above results.

== Multiplicity along a subvariety ==
Let <math>(A, \mathfrak{m})</math> be the [[local ring]] of a variety ''X'' at a closed subvariety ''V'' [[codimension]] ''n'' (for example, ''V'' can be a [[closed point]]). Then <math>\operatorname{length}_A(A/\mathfrak{m}^t)</math> is a polynomial of degree ''n'' in ''t'' for large ''t''; i.e., it can be written as <math>{ e(A)^n \over n!}  t^n + </math> the lower-degree terms and the integer <math>e(A)</math> is called the [[multiplicity of a module|multiplicity]] of ''A''.

The Segre class <math>s(V, X)</math> of <math>V \subset X</math> encodes this multiplicity: the coefficient of <math>[V]</math> in <math>s(V, X)</math> is <math>e(A)</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|1998|loc=Example 4.3.1.}}</ref>
